random_page_cost controls the planner’s estimate of the cost of a non‑sequential (random) disk page fetch; lowering it makes index scans look cheaper and raising it makes index scans look more expensive. Default: 4.0 [1].

effective_io_concurrency controls the number of concurrent disk I/O operations PostgreSQL expects it can issue (it increases how many I/O requests a session attempts in parallel); currently it only affects bitmap heap scans. Default: 1 on supported systems, otherwise 0 [3].

hw6.answer: Index-only scans additionally require that the heap pages involved be marked “all visible” in the visibility map so the scan can skip heap fetches. Vacuum (including autovacuum) maintains and updates that visibility map; if pages aren’t marked all-visible (i.e. vacuum hasn’t cleared old dead tuples and set the map), index-only scans won’t be usable even with a covering index [1][3].

hw9.answer:
shared_buffers: default ~128MB (min 128kB). For a dedicated DB server with ≥1GB RAM, a reasonable starting value is about 25% of system RAM; some workloads benefit from larger values but >40% is unlikely to help; large shared_buffers often require increasing max_wal_size [1].
effective_cache_size: this is the planner’s assumption about the effective size of the disk cache available to a single query; it affects cost estimates (higher → index scans more likely, lower → seq scans more likely). It should reflect shared_buffers plus the portion of the OS cache PostgreSQL can use and expected concurrency. It does not allocate or reserve memory—only used for planning. Default is 4GB [2].
